note: Per-state net-metering briefing + New England REC market reference for array operators. Refreshed daily by a research agent; every figure is sourced — always verify against the linked authority before relying on it. Array Operator invoices bill from the offtaker's real settled-bill rate regardless.

vt.name: Vermont
vt.comp: Blended residential ≈ $0.2071/kWh (raised from $0.1839 by the May 29, 2026 biennial update, now in effect for permits Aug 1, 2026 onward); Category I (≤15 kW) effective ≈ $0.1571/kWh after the siting charge rose 4¢ → 5¢.
vt.how: Rates are set by the PUC's biennial update; an array's rate locks ~10 years from its permit, then rolls to the blended rate. Small systems add +$0.01/kWh, or +$0.03/kWh if RECs go to the utility.
vt.note: Group / offsite (community) net metering is being phased out under H.289 — existing arrays keep running. Gov. Scott signed S.202 (Act 84) on June 16, 2026 (effective July 1) legalizing plug-in 'balcony' solar up to 1,200 W AC per meter, though it can't be combined with an existing net-metering system. Separately, the Vermont PUC on Aug 28, 2026 approved a 5.5% Green Mountain Power distribution rate increase effective Oct 1, 2026 (Case 26-0096-TF) — below the 7.5% GMP requested — approving about $113M of 'resilience' infrastructure spending (roughly a third of GMP's $341M request) and citing affordability. Gov. Scott vetoed H.710 on June 17, 2026 — a permitting/decommissioning bill that would have narrowed PUC 'single plant' determinations for adjacent small solar — drawing criticism from Renewable Energy Vermont. The July 31, 2026 CPG-application deadline to lock the prior framework has now passed; systems permitted Aug 1, 2026 onward take the updated blended rate (≈ $0.2071/kWh) with the higher 5¢/kWh siting charge. Separately, on Sept 9, 2026 the PUC issued an order opening an investigation to update Commission Rule 5.100 (net-metering construction and operation), with a stakeholder workshop set for Oct 2, 2026 at 9:30 a.m.
vt.reg: PUC Case 26-0291-INV — 2026 biennial update, order May 29, 2026 (the 7th consecutive Category I cut).

rec.program: Vermont RES + NEPOOL-GIS Class I (out-of-state sale)
rec.owner_path: Net-metered systems that transfer RECs to the utility earn a +$0.03/kWh adjustor; systems that keep RECs can sell Class I certificates into NEPOOL (or have a verifier/aggregator do it).
rec.how: Vermont's Renewable Energy Standard (rewritten by H.289) drives utility demand for RECs. Small net-metered arrays often leave the certificate with the utility for the rate adjustor; larger or offsite systems may retain and sell them. Tracking is via NEPOOL-GIS with an Independent Verifier.
rec.acp_or_cap: State RES compliance; Class I ACP set by the demanding state's program (MA/CT often set the regional ceiling).

nh.name: New Hampshire
nh.comp: NEM 2.0 credits exports at ≈ 85% of retail (100% of supply + transmission + 25% of distribution). Eversource retail ≈ $0.25/kWh.
nh.how: The NEM 2.0 credit formula is locked through Jan 1, 2041 (Docket DE 16-576) — unusually long-term stability for the region.
nh.note: Three 2026 laws extend the edges of net metering: SB 540 (signed July 2, 2026, Chapter 262; effective Jan 1, 2027) legalizes portable plug-in 'balcony' solar up to 1,200 W AC per customer, exempting it from interconnection agreements, utility approval and net-metering rules; HB 1718 (signed July 10, 2026, Chapter 309) directs the Dept. of Energy and PUC to credit exports from renewable-charged batteries; and SB 538 (signed July 10, 2026, Chapter 315, effective Sept 8, 2026) locks the current net-metering credit for 20 years for municipal solar projects up to 5 MW already in the interconnection queue. Separately, the NH PUC approved Eversource's default energy service rate at 14.009¢/kWh effective Aug 1, 2026 through January.
nh.reg: NH PUC affirmed the Eversource rate case (monthly customer charge ≈ $14 → $19.81, ROE 9.5%) but on reconsideration (Jan 6, 2026 order) threw out the automatic annual increases; the Dept. of Energy has appealed the alternative-regulation framework (Docket DE 24-070) to the NH Supreme Court.

rec.program: NH RPS Class I / Class II (solar) + NEPOOL-GIS
rec.price_display: ≈ $34–40 / MWh (Class I); Class II solar often trades near Class I
rec.owner_path: Owners typically register with NEPOOL-GIS and use an Independent Monitor (often the utility for net-metered systems) to report production so RECs can be minted and sold.
rec.how: New Hampshire's RPS requires Class I (new renewables) and a Class II solar carve-out. Solar arrays that register and report can sell certificates; net-metering credits and REC sales are separate revenue streams.
rec.acp_or_cap: NH RPS ACP rates are published annually by the Dept. of Energy / PUC.

me.name: Maine
me.comp: Net Energy Billing (NEB) — 1:1 retail-rate credits for rooftop solar. CMP ≈ $0.27/kWh, Versant ≈ $0.32/kWh; credits roll monthly and true up annually.
me.how: Rooftop NEB is protected; LD 1777 halted new community-solar NEB and added monthly charges on existing community arrays, with a successor front-of-meter program (DSES) to be designed in 2026.
me.note: LD 1777 bars new community-solar NEB and adds monthly charges on existing arrays ($2.80/kW-AC for 1–3 MW-AC, $6/kW-AC for 3–5 MW-AC) effective Jan 1, 2026; the successor program is now taking shape: DOER published a draft Front-of-the-Meter Distributed Energy Resources (FTM DER) program proposal in late August 2026 for projects excluded from NEB, held a Sept 2 webinar, took written comments through Sept 11, and must submit a program design to the MPUC by Sept 30, 2026. CMP's refundable temporary distribution rates took effect July 1, 2026 (~$4/mo bill decrease, no distribution-charge increase through April 2027) while its one-year rate case is reviewed by the MPUC. Separately, on July 20, 2026 the Department of Energy Resources filed the state's first competitive energy-storage solicitation seeking up to 360 MW toward Maine's statutory 400 MW-by-2030 goal, with the MPUC given up to 120 days to review before a formal RFP issues.
me.reg: Maine PUC (MPUC). LD 1792 reversed a 2025 cost-allocation increase; tariff rates are set through 2046 (Dockets 2019-00197, 2022-00185). CMP residential Standard Offer (supply) is 12.721¢/kWh for 2026.

rec.owner_path: NEB credits are the primary owner revenue; RECs for qualifying generation can still be registered and sold if not claimed by the program counterparty — check the project's tariff / PPA.
rec.how: Maine participates in NEPOOL-GIS. Class I RECs from eligible renewable facilities can supply Maine or other New England RPS markets when dual-qualified. Community NEB reforms (LD 1777) do not erase existing certificate eligibility.
rec.acp_or_cap: Maine RPS ACP published by the PUC / Legislature schedule.

ma.name: Massachusetts
ma.comp: 1:1 retail-rate net metering for residential ≤ 25 kW (Class I) — credits ≈ $0.2836/kWh (Eversource), ≈ $0.32/kWh (National Grid).
ma.how: On top of net metering, SMART 3.0 (PY2026) pays a flat $0.03/kWh incentive (residential ≤ 25 kW; $0.06/kWh low-income).
ma.note: DPU Docket 25-200 (delivery rate design) is examining whether to reduce the value of net-metering credits; no changes have been ordered and existing systems are expected to be grandfathered. The DPU approved DOER's redesigned SMART 3.0 program (225 CMR 28.00) on May 19, 2026, replacing the declining-block model with annually adjusted incentive blocks; Program Year 2026 carries 600 MW-AC of capacity, and the 20-year ratepayer cost for 2025–2026 projects was revised down to roughly $4.5 billion on lower-than-expected enrollment. As of mid-July 2026 the SMART 3.0/2.0 model tariffs remain pending in DPU Docket 25-175; DOER is issuing Preliminary — not Final — Statements of Qualification, and incentive payments do not start until the tariffs are approved. Separately, the Massachusetts Senate passed omnibus energy bill S.3143 on July 1, 2026 and it went to a conference committee (led by Sen. Mike Barrett) to reconcile with the House's H.5175; it leaves residential and customer-sited rooftop net metering intact but would reduce net-metering credit values for larger standalone non-residential facilities (~$75M in projected ratepayer savings over ten years) — a change cited as a factor easing regional Class I REC forwards. Key disputes (including a proposed $1B Mass Save cut) remained unresolved and, as of late September 2026, the bill was still stuck in conference with no deal — prompting Gov. Healey to say her administration is weighing direct relief for households heading into winter. Separately, Gov. Healey signed a data-center executive order on Sept 8, 2026 requiring new data centers to meet demand with clean energy, obtain local approval, and cover their own grid costs to protect ratepayers — advocates urged it as a model for the pending energy-affordability bill.
ma.reg: MA Dept. of Public Utilities (DPU); the SMART incentive is administered by DOER.

rec.program: MA RPS Class I (+ legacy SREC I/II for remaining terms); SMART systems typically transfer RECs to the utility/program
rec.price_display: Class I ≈ $34–40 / MWh; legacy SRECs much higher while terms last
rec.owner_path: SMART-enrolled systems usually assign RECs to the utility as a condition of the incentive. Legacy SREC I/II systems still mint SRECs until their term ends (or Q4 2027, whichever first), then roll to Class I. Independent systems can sell Class I via NEPOOL-GIS.
rec.how: Massachusetts is the regional demand anchor for Class I RECs. The Class I minimum standard keeps stepping up each year (plus solar carve-outs). The $40/MWh Class I ACP (fixed since 2023) is the hard ceiling. 1 REC = 1 MWh; minting is on the NEPOOL-GIS trimester cycle with a lag, via GIS + Independent Verifier.
rec.acp_or_cap: MA Class I ACP is fixed at $40/MWh (225 CMR 14.08, unchanged since Compliance Year 2023) — it caps the market, since suppliers can pay the ACP instead of buying RECs.

ct.name: Connecticut
ct.comp: No net metering — the RRES Netting Tariff (PURA). Pick Netting (retail-rate credits, 20 yr) or Buy-All (fixed ≈ $0.3289/kWh for 2026 enrollments, 20 yr). Plus a +$0.0402/kWh Solar Energy Adjustment in 2026.
ct.how: Whichever option you choose at enrollment is locked for 20 years; Eversource and United Illuminating administer it identically.
ct.note: Utility-vs-state tension is running hot: Connecticut (Gov. Lamont, AG Tong, DEEP, OCC) filed a FERC complaint in June 2026 to strip the ~0.50% RTO transmission incentive adder Eversource and UI collect (projected ~$4.5M/yr in CT savings), and on June 30 the two utilities sued the state in federal court challenging Public Act 25-173 (SB 4). Eversource also asked PURA to keep ~300,000 pages of its rate-case filing confidential. On the procurement side, Eversource opened the Program Year 5 (2026) Non-Residential Renewable Energy Solutions (NRES) August solicitation on Aug 3, 2026, accepting competitive bids for zero-emission projects from 200 kW up to 5,000 kW-AC through Sept 14, 2026. On August 14, 2026 Acadia Center was granted intervenor status in Eversource's pending distribution rate case, challenging the utility's requested 10.25% return on equity as 'out of step with ROEs nationwide' and advocating performance-based ratemaking. Near-term prices are falling: a Sept 17, 2026 CT Mirror report notes Eversource standard-service supply dropped to 11.577¢/kWh on July 1, 2026 and a public-benefits bill credit of roughly $30–34/month runs through April 2027 (driven largely by long-term Millstone and Seabrook nuclear contracts), even as Eversource's pending distribution case seeks a double-digit increase for July 2027.
ct.reg: Public Utilities Regulatory Authority (PURA) — RRES replaced net metering in 2022. Eversource filed a rate case on July 14, 2026 seeking ~$451M in distribution revenue (~11% residential), rising to a headline ~$727M (~18%) once ~$1B of 2018–2023 storm costs are included; new rates would take effect July 1, 2027. Separately, PURA's July 29, 2026 final storm-cost decision approved about $861M in deferred 2018–2023 storm costs while rejecting ~$400M in retrospective carrying charges, with roughly $668M to be securitized. Standard-service supply rates fell July 1, 2026 (Eversource to ≈11.58¢/kWh, UI to ≈11.99¢/kWh), and a May 1, 2026 Rate Adjustment Mechanism decision cut interim delivery rates.

rec.program: CT RPS Class I + NEPOOL-GIS (often dual-qualified with MA)
rec.price_display: ≈ $34–40 / MWh (Class I; often co-moves with MA)
rec.owner_path: RRES / Buy-All program terms usually assign renewable attributes to the utility or program. Standalone / merchant systems that keep attributes can sell Class I RECs regionally.
rec.how: Connecticut Class I prices tend to move with Massachusetts; both can supply dual-qualified NEPOOL contracts. Tracking is NEPOOL-GIS.
rec.acp_or_cap: CT Class I ACP published under the state's RPS schedule.

ri.name: Rhode Island
ri.comp: Net metering ≈ 80% of retail (≈ $0.232/kWh) for new systems, 125% annual cap, protected through 2039. The separate REG program pays ≈ $0.2723/kWh for 15 years.
ri.how: Net metering credits your excess up to 125% of on-site use; the Renewable Energy Growth (REG) program pays a fixed rate for all production instead.
ri.note: The 2026 legislative session (ended June 11) killed a proposed solar 'grid access fee' on systems ≥ 1 MW but set up lower virtual-net-metering compensation for large projects and lowers the net-metering program cap from 275 MW toward 175 MW by 2031. The OER and PUC are reviewing both programs; a CRNM v2 community-solar tier (40 MW cap) is expected in 2026–2027. A separate net-metering tariff docket (25-50-EL), updating RI Energy's Net Metering Provision to reflect the 2025 changes to Excess Renewable Net Metering Credit valuation, reached its Division closing memo on June 22, 2026 with a final PUC order still pending. On August 14, 2026 RI Energy filed a further revised net-metering provision (Docket 26-30-EL, proposed effective Sept 13, 2026) that lowers the aggregate ground-mount remote-net-metering cap from 275 MW to 175 MW, extends the qualifying-project deadline from July 1, 2030 to Dec 31, 2032, and adds an optional 'Fixed Renewable Net Metering Credit' of 19¢/kWh (escalating 2.75%/yr from 2028) over 25 years for public, educational, hospital, community-remote and C&I systems; the PUC must approve an implementing tariff by Dec 1, 2026.
ri.reg: RI PUC + Office of Energy Resources (OER). RI Energy's base distribution rate case (Docket 25-45-GE) was decided on Aug 21, 2026: the PUC approved a modified increase of ~$44.1M electric and ~$93.7M gas — well below the requested ~$65.9M electric / ~$114.7M gas. RI Energy made its compliance filing Aug 27, 2026 and the new rates took effect Sept 1, 2026, raising a typical residential electric bill about $7.78/month (~4.83%) in the first year. The Commission held the allowed return on equity at 9.275% (rejecting the utility's bid to raise it to 10.75%) and, siding with the Attorney General, secured roughly $170M in accelerated bill credits for ratepayers from Oct 2026 through Sept 2027. On July 23, 2026 Gov. McKee signed Executive Order 26-05 declaring an energy-affordability emergency and directing ~$28M of RGGI reserves toward residential bill relief (pending PUC approval); the order was filed into the rate-case docket Aug 6. Separately, on July 24, 2026 RI Energy filed (Docket 26-27-EL) to raise its residential Last Resort Service supply rate to 17.029¢/kWh for the Oct 1, 2026–Mar 31, 2027 winter period, roughly 15% above the prior winter, pending PUC approval. Executive Order 26-01 directs OER to complete a net-metering / REG review by Oct 1, 2026.

rec.program: RI RES Class I + NEPOOL-GIS; REG often transfers RECs to the utility
rec.owner_path: REG program participants typically transfer RECs as part of the fixed-price offtake. Net-metered systems that retain attributes can register and sell Class I certificates.
rec.how: Rhode Island's Renewable Energy Standard creates Class I demand. RECs are tracked in NEPOOL-GIS and may dual-qualify for other New England markets.
rec.acp_or_cap: RI RES ACP rates set under state statute / OER schedule.

rec_market.headline: New England REC market
rec_market.summary: Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs) are the tradable proof that 1 MWh of renewable electricity was generated. Across New England they are issued and tracked in NEPOOL-GIS, typically one quarter after generation. Class I RECs (new renewables, post-1997 facilities) are the main commodity solar operators care about; MA and CT demand often set the regional price. SRECs are a legacy Massachusetts solar carve-out that still pays higher while individual terms last, then rolls to Class I.

class_i.label: NEPOOL Class I (region)
class_i.note: Indicative broker range for dual-qualified New England Class I. Not a live bid. The nearest vintages remain close to the $40 ceiling in a sixth straight undersupplied year, and Power Advisory's August 2026 update shows forwards (Marex Spectron, as of Aug 13, 2026) still near the cap, with only mild erosion into the low-to-mid $30s further out after Connecticut's SB4 (July 2025) and the Massachusetts Senate's S.3143 (July 2026); forwards are still expected to hold above $30. Separately, NECEC Quebec hydro (delivering since January 2026) is expected to cover nearly all of the Massachusetts Clean Energy Standard (CES ACP $35) requirement in CY2026, leaving Class I certificates banked for Class I compliance. July 2026 broker quotes (Gridwealth) pegged MA Class I at $38–$42 with Competitive Energy Services describing the market 'trading just below $40' (live Xpansiv/MassCEC feeds are subscriber-gated). The MA Class I ACP remains $40/MWh (225 CMR 14.08, flat since Compliance Year 2023 — confirmed unchanged for 2026), and RI has aligned its ACP to $40 flat, so the ceiling is now uniform across MA, CT and RI; do not confuse it with the separate Clean Peak (CPES) ACP (~$65). The MA Class I minimum standard is roughly 30% of retail sales for 2026. Connecticut's Class I RPS obligation drops from 32% to 25% for 2026 (and excludes new biomass/methane as of Oct 1, 2025), shifting some supply toward the higher-priced NH market. Prices have historically swung from single digits to the cap.
class_i.mint_lag: Issued quarterly, roughly one quarter after generation (e.g. Q1 generation mints mid-year).

products.name: Class I REC
products.note: Primary New England renewable commodity. Solar, wind, eligible hydro, etc.

products.name: MA SREC I / II (legacy)
products.price_display: Much higher than Class I while term lasts
products.note: Closed solar carve-outs. Systems roll to Class I after 10-year/40-quarter term or end of Q4 2027 (whichever first).

products.name: SMART attributes (MA)
products.note: SMART incentive typically requires transferring RECs/attributes — the $/kWh incentive is the compensation path, not open-market REC sales.

rec_market.operator_tip: If your arrays already report into NEPOOL-GIS (or a verifier does it for you), check whether YOU still own the certificates. Many net-metering / SMART / REG programs transfer RECs to the utility. Certificates you still own are real money — typically tens of dollars per MWh of generation.
